transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-25 14:00 UTC | Duration: 50 mins | Attendees: Alex Kim, Priya Desai, Marco Alvarez, Jordan Lee, Samira Noor, Evan Brooks

Summary (auto): quick practice session, 3 role-swap rounds, focused on opening, product narrative, and technical fallback demo.

00:00 Alex Kim: okay everyone, uh thanks for carving out time for flight deck practice, this is the 15-minute rapid cycle plus two longer role swaps, we're aiming to tighten the handoff between AE and SE.
00:18 Jordan Lee: cool, sounds good. I'm gonna timebox interruptions to two per demo.
00:25 Priya Desai: yep, I'll start as SE for round one, Alex is AE; Marco will observe and note timing.
00:33 Alex Kim: perfect. opening line — "Redwood helps you ship predictable LLM inference at production scale, with predictable latency and cost controls" — try it.
00:45 Priya Desai: "Redwood helps teams ship LLM features faster by unifying runtime across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments, and giving you levers like batching and caching to control cost" — mmm, I slipped on the levers phrasing.
01:02 Samira Noor: maybe say 'levers like intelligent batching, prefix caching, and quantization profiles' so it's crisp.
01:20 Alex Kim: good, callout: when they ask about 'how do you beat Open AI on price', we need the latency-vs-cost script. Priya, take that.
01:35 Priya Desai: ok, short script: we position for production economics — you can tradeoff latency for unit cost via batching, quantization, and routing policies. For ultra-low latency we recommend dedicated pools and prefix KV cache; for lower cost we recommend quantization and larger batch windows.
01:58 Jordan Lee: small nit: don't say "KV cash" — we had a bad auto-caption on that. say "KV cache" clearly.
02:10 Marco Alvarez: noted. also highlight the routing fallback: if a dedicated pool is saturated we auto-fall back to a compatible small model in the same family to preserve availability. that's important for reliability questions.
02:28 Evan Brooks: can we get a one-liner for the marketing deck about model fallback?
02:35 Priya Desai: "Automatic model fallback keeps your app online by routing to compatible variants when capacity is constrained, preserving latency SLOs while limiting quality regressions".
02:50 Samira Noor: good. next, role-swap round 1: Jordan will play a mid-market PM who cares about security and SSO.
03:05 Jordan Lee (as PM): hi, we have strict SSO and audit requirements, how does Redwood handle SAML and audit logs?
03:14 Alex Kim (AE): great question — short answer: we support SAML/SSO, SSO integrations with IdPs, RBAC at token level, and audit logs with retention policies. for regulated customers we also offer private deploy with customer KMS/HSM.
03:35 Jordan (as PM): can you be specific about SOC2?
03:40 Priya Desai: we are SOC 2 Type II compliant (note: double-check latest cert), we surface audit logs in the console and you can forward logs to your SIEM. we also have support for customer-managed KMS in private deployments.
03:58 Jordan Lee: there was a hesitation — make a note to always confirm certificate date before calls.
04:06 Marco Alvarez: action: add a small card to slide 6 that says 'SOC 2 status: see compliance pack' and link it.
04:18 Alex Kim: round two: latency objection from a startup that runs conversational search. Evan will play.
04:30 Evan Brooks (as Startup CTO): our priority is sub-100ms generation for short queries, can you do that and at what cost?
04:40 Priya Desai: short answer: depends on model size and sequence length; for sub-100ms we lean into dedicated pools, memory-optimized GPU configs, and aggressive KV cache warmups; costs will be higher, but through routing you can serve heavier queries on dedicated and fallback less latency sensitive requests to cheaper variants.
04:58 Evan: what about caching cold-starts?
05:03 Priya: warmup strategies include prefix caching and predictive prefetch; also continuous batching — but be careful in wording: continuous batching reduces cost but increases tail latency for singleton requests.
05:20 Samira Noor: there's a concise line: 'we automate warmups and cache priming so your hot paths hit <10ms KV cache where appropriate' — again quantify only when you have the benchmark.
05:36 Alex Kim: note — link to perf spreadsheet in the follow-up.
05:45 Jordan Lee: round three, procurement/finance lead: wants pricing commitment vs usage variability.
05:53 Evan (as Fin): do you have reserved capacity and how does billing work?
06:00 Priya Desai: yes, we offer Dedicated reserved pools (monthly/annual commits) for predictable throughput and a hosted usage-based API for flexible consumption. if you need price predictability we push to dedicated with commit discounts and burst policy controls.
06:20 Evan: any penalties for overage?
06:24 Alex Kim: typically overage is billed at published overage rates unless negotiated. procurement asks we should hand off to solutions for committed sizing sessions.
06:36 Marco Alvarez: quick practical demo: show the console -> create a route -> pin model version -> enable canary rollout. Priya will drive the UI.
06:48 Priya Desai: (screen share simulated) slide notes: open console, create route, model catalog select 'redwood-2-7b-quant', set rollout 10% canary, autoscale min 2 GPUs. navigation slightly choppy here — practice flow: go slower through clicks.
07:12 Samira Noor: audience wants to see failure demo — can we simulate a node eviction and show fallback?
07:18 Priya: yes, scripted demo: trigger capacity drain, show request hitting fallback variant, observe logs/traces in the console. Marco: you should prep a short script and a pre-recorded clip for field use.
07:30 Marco Alvarez: will do.
07:33 Alex Kim: time check — 10 minutes left, we'll do rapid role-swap with interrupts.
07:40 Jordan Lee: one quick objection that often surfaces: 'We have to host on-prem due to data residency' — how do we position private vs dedicated?
07:50 Priya Desai: position: private gives full network isolation and customer-managed KMS; dedicated is managed but isolated tenancy; both support model pinning and rollouts but private adds the option for on-prem or VPC-only control. emphasize tradeoffs: operational overhead vs SLA/backups.
08:12 Evan Brooks: competitor angle: how do we compare to Anthropic's offering?
08:18 Alex Kim: be crisp: Anthropic is model-first; Redwood is serving-first — we separate serving guarantees, routing, and unit economics. avoid technical slam, instead emphasize production controls and observability.
08:36 Samira Noor: can we capture two sample scripts: (1) 'Anthropic competitor' short rebuttal and (2) 'OpenAI price question' script — add to playbook.
08:48 Priya: yes, I'll draft both.
08:52 Jordan Lee: recording a 60-90s battlecard clip would be great for new reps.
09:00 Marco Alvarez: last exercise: AE stumbles on the pricing question and SE has 30s to rescue with the routing/layered controls script.
09:12 Alex Kim: go.
09:16 Alex Kim (AE): "their price is lower, why would we pay more to Redwood?"
09:20 Priya Desai (SE): "short answer: unit cost alone doesn't capture app-level economics — we reduce ops toil, avoid downtime with automatic fallback and can reduce total spend via caching and quantization; we'll run a cost model specific to your workload."
09:36 Alex Kim: good rescue. note: use 'total cost of ownership' phrasing.
09:42 Jordan Lee: we ran out of time for the longer failure script — add to next steps.
09:50 Alex Kim: recap — action items captured; we'll push slides and playbook links; test recording planned. Thanks everyone.

Auto Notes: shared artifacts: Flight Deck v2 slides, enablement playbook, perf spreadsheet. Follow-up scheduled 2025-10-07 for role-swap continuation.

End of transcript.
